newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan traders rejects Ssangyong naphtha price rise.
newsitem.headline: Japan traders rejects Ssangyong naphtha price rise.

text.p: Japanese naphtha traders on Friday rejected a South Korean refiner's proposal to raise prices of its supplies in the middle of the term year, calling it "totally unacceptable."

South Korea's Ssangyong Oil Refining Co has asked its Japanese clients to consider accepting an unspecified increase in term naphtha premiums for annual contracts that started in January, traders said.
The current term price is set at the mean of Japanese quotes minus $1.50 per tonne for six of the seven Japanese buyers, and minus $3.00 a tonne for one buyer, traders said.
Generally, contract prices are only negotiated between prior to the beginning of each term year, traders said.
"It's totally out of the question to try to change terms of the contract half way through the contract year," one Japanese trader said.
Japanese customers -- three oil firms and four trading houses -- said they have told Ssangyong they are rejecting the proposal and are waiting for a reply.
Traders in Tokyo said the South Korean firm had threatened not to provide August naphtha cargoes if Japanese buyers did not accept the proposal, a charge Ssangyong denies.

"We (Ssangyong) are not gangsters... We have to supply the cargoes. But our proposal to raise the premium, or adjust the premium, was to avoid any difficulties in contract negotiations for the next term year," a Ssangyong naphtha trader said.
He added the firm would deliver August-lifting cargoes regardless of Japanese clients' reaction to the proposal.
Without a revision, premiums for next term year would be drastically higher than this year, he said.
Japanese buyers are due to buy roughly a combined 1.2 million tonnes of naphtha from Ssangyong this year.

As naphtha stockpiles are currently high in Japan due to brisk domestic production, a possible disruption in supplies would only have a small impact on the operations of petrochemical firms, traders said.
Record-high premiums for Middle Eastern term naphtha set earlier this year, probably encouraged Ssangyong to seek higher prices for its supplies, traders said.
Saudi Arabia's A-180 naphtha price, for instance, was set at $17.00 per tonne over the Aramco formula for the second-half of 1997, compared with a $6.50 premium for the January-June period.
The rise came on the back of growing naphtha demand from petrochemical plants that are springing up across Asia.
In Asia, naphtha is mainly used to manufacture ethylene and propylene, the building blocks of various petrochemical products.
